vsm1.4:21.1: Now, with the clause, And not overlook any of the directions for development (III.28),
vsm1.4:21.2: the time has come for the detailed exposition of all meditation subjects, starting with the earth kasiṇa.
vsm1.4:22.1: When a bhikkhu has thus severed the lesser impediments,
vsm1.4:22.2: then, on his return from his alms round after his meal
vsm1.4:22.3: and after he has got rid of drowsiness due to the meal,
vsm1.4:22.4: he should sit down comfortably in a secluded place
vsm1.4:22.5: and apprehend the sign in earth that is either made up or not made up.
vsm1.4:22.7: “One who is learning the earth kasiṇa apprehends the sign in earth that is either made up or not made up;
vsm1.4:22.10: with a periphery, not without a periphery;
vsm1.4:22.12: either the size of a bushel (suppa) or the size of a saucer (sarāva).
vsm1.4:22.13: He sees to it that that sign is well apprehended, well attended to, well defined.
vsm1.4:22.14: Having well apprehended that sign, well attended to it, and well defined it,
vsm1.4:22.16: and perceiving it as a treasure,
vsm1.4:22.19: he anchors his mind to that object,
vsm1.4:22.20: thinking, ‘Surely in this way I shall be freed from aging and death.’
vsm1.4:22.21: Secluded from sense desires … he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna …”
vsm1.4:23.1:
Herein, when in a previous becoming a man has gone forth into homelessness
in the Dispensation or outside it with the rishis’ going forth
vsm1.4:23.2: and has already produced the jhāna tetrad or pentad on the earth kasiṇa,
vsm1.4:23.3: and so has such merit and the support of past practice of jhāna as well,
vsm1.4:23.4: then the sign arises in him on earth that is not made up, that is to say, on a ploughed area or on a threshing floor,
vsm1.4:23.5: as in the Elder Mallaka’s case.
vsm1.4:23.6: It seems that while that venerable one was looking at a ploughed area the sign arose in him the size of that area.
vsm1.4:23.7: He extended it and attained the jhāna pentad.
vsm1.4:23.8: Then by establishing insight with the jhāna as the basis for it,
vsm1.4:24.1: But when a man has had no such previous practice,
vsm1.4:24.2:
he should make a kasiṇa, guarding against the four faults of a kasiṇa and not overlooking
any of the directions for the meditation subject learnt from the teacher.
vsm1.4:24.3: Now, the four faults of the earth kasiṇa are due to the intrusion of blue, yellow, red or white.
vsm1.4:24.4: So instead of using clay of such colours,
vsm1.4:24.5: he should make the kasiṇa of clay like that in the stream of the Gangā, which is the colour of the dawn.
vsm1.4:24.6: And he should make it not in the middle of the monastery in a place where novices, etc., are about
vsm1.4:24.7: but on the confines of the monastery in a screened place, either under an overhanging rock or in a leaf hut.
vsm1.4:24.8: He can make it either portable or as a fixture.
vsm1.4:25.1: Of these, a portable one should be made by tying rags of leather or matting onto four sticks
vsm1.4:25.2:
and smearing thereon a disk of the size already mentioned, using clay picked clean of grass,
roots, gravel, and sand, and well kneaded.
vsm1.4:25.3: At the time of the preliminary work it should be laid on the ground and looked at.
vsm1.4:25.4: A fixture should be made by knocking stakes into the ground in the form of a lotus calyx, lacing them over with creepers.
vsm1.4:25.6: then other clay should be put underneath
vsm1.4:25.7: and a disk a span and four fingers across made on top of that with the quite pure dawn-coloured clay.
vsm1.4:25.8: For it was with reference only to measurement that it was said above either the size of a bushel or the size of a saucer (§22).
vsm1.4:25.9: But that is bounded, not unbounded was said to show its delimitedness.
vsm1.4:26.1: So, having thus made it delimited and of the size prescribed,
vsm1.4:26.2: he should scrape it down with a stone trowel—a wooden trowel turns it a bad colour, so that should not be employed—
vsm1.4:26.3: and make it as even as the surface of a drum.
vsm1.4:26.4: Then he should sweep the place out and have a bath.
vsm1.4:26.5:
On his return he should seat himself on a well-covered chair with legs a span and four fingers high, prepared in a place
that is two and a half cubits that is, two and a half times elbow to finger-tip from the kasiṇa disk.
vsm1.4:26.6: For the kasiṇa does not appear plainly to him if he sits further off than that;
vsm1.4:26.7: and if he sits nearer than that, faults in the kasiṇa appear.
vsm1.4:26.8: If he sits higher up, he has to look at it with his neck bent; and if he sits lower down, his knees ache.
vsm1.4:27.1: So, after seating himself in the way stated,
vsm1.4:27.2: he should review the dangers in sense desires in the way beginning, “Sense desires give little enjoyment” (M I 91)
vsm1.4:27.3: and arouse longing for the escape from sense desires, for the renunciation that is the means to the surmounting of all suffering.
vsm1.4:27.4: He should next arouse joy of happiness by recollecting the special qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha;
vsm1.4:27.5: then awe by thinking, “Now, this is the way of renunciation entered upon by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples”;
vsm1.4:27.6: and then eagerness by thinking, “In this way I shall surely come to know the taste of the bliss of seclusion.”
vsm1.4:27.7: After that he should open his eyes moderately, apprehend the sign, and so proceed to develop it.
vsm1.4:28.1: If he opens his eyes too wide, they get fatigued
vsm1.4:28.2: and the disk becomes too obvious,
vsm1.4:28.3: which prevents the sign becoming apparent to him.
vsm1.4:28.4: If he opens them too little, the disk is not obvious enough,
vsm1.4:28.6: which also prevents the sign becoming apparent to him.
vsm1.4:28.7:
So he should develop it by apprehending the sign (nimitta), keeping his eyes open moderately,
as if he were seeing the reflection of his face (mukha-nimitta) on the surface of a looking-glass.
vsm1.4:29.1: The colour should not be reviewed.
vsm1.4:29.2: The characteristic should not be given attention.
vsm1.4:29.3: But rather, while not ignoring the colour,
vsm1.4:29.4:
attention should be given by setting the mind on the name concept as the most outstanding mental datum,
relegating the colour to the position of a property of its physical support.
vsm1.4:29.5:
That conceptual state can be called by anyone he likes among the names for earth (pathavī) such
as “earth” (pathavī), “the Great One” (mahī), “the Friendly One” (medinī),
vsm1.4:29.6: “ground” (bhūmi), “the Provider of Wealth” (vasudhā), “the Bearer of Wealth” (vasudharā), etc.,
vsm1.4:29.7: whichever suits his manner of perception.
vsm1.4:29.8: Still “earth” is also a name that is obvious, so it can be developed with the obvious one by saying “earth, earth.”
vsm1.4:29.9: It should be adverted to now with eyes open, now with eyes shut.
vsm1.4:29.10:
And he should go on developing it in this way a hundred times, a thousand times, and even
more than that, until the learning sign arises.
vsm1.4:30.1: When, while he is developing it in this way,
vsm1.4:30.2: it comes into focus as he adverts with his eyes shut exactly as it does with his eyes open,
vsm1.4:30.3: then the learning sign is said to have been produced.
vsm1.4:30.4: After its production he should no longer sit in that place;
vsm1.4:30.5: he should return to his own quarters and go on developing it sitting there.
vsm1.4:30.6: But in order to avoid the delay of foot washing, a pair of single-soled sandals and a walking stick are desirable.
vsm1.4:30.7: Then if the new concentration vanishes through some unsuitable encounter,
vsm1.4:30.8: he can put his sandals on, take his walking stick,
vsm1.4:30.9: and go back to the place to re-apprehend the sign there.
vsm1.4:30.10: When he returns he should seat himself comfortably
vsm1.4:30.11: and develop it by reiterated reaction to it and by striking at it with thought and applied thought.
vsm1.4:31.1: As he does so, the hindrances eventually become suppressed,
vsm1.4:31.3: the mind becomes concentrated with access concentration,
vsm1.4:31.5: The difference between the earlier learning sign and the counterpart sign is this.
vsm1.4:31.6: In the learning sign any fault in the kasiṇa is apparent.
vsm1.4:31.7:
But the counterpart sign appears as if breaking out from the learning sign, and a hundred times, a thousand
times more purified, like a looking-glass disk drawn from its case, like a mother-of-pearl dish well washed,
like the moon’s disk coming out from behind a cloud, like cranes against a thunder cloud.
vsm1.4:31.8: But it has neither colour nor shape;
vsm1.4:31.10:
it would be cognizable by the eye, gross, susceptible of comprehension by insight—(see
XX.2f.) and stamped with the three characteristics.
vsm1.4:31.11: But it is not like that.
vsm1.4:31.12: For it is born only of perception in one who has obtained concentration, being a mere mode of appearance.
vsm1.4:31.13: But as soon as it arises the hindrances are quite suppressed,
vsm1.4:31.15: and the mind becomes concentrated in access concentration.
vsm1.4:32.1: Now, concentration is of two kinds, that is to say, access concentration and absorption concentration:
vsm1.4:32.2: the mind becomes concentrated in two ways, that is, on the plane of access and on the plane of obtainment.
vsm1.4:32.3: Herein, the mind becomes concentrated on the plane of access by the abandonment of the hindrances,
vsm1.4:32.4: and on the plane of obtainment by the manifestation of the jhāna factors.
vsm1.4:33.1: The difference between the two kinds of concentration is this.
vsm1.4:33.2: The factors are not strong in access.
vsm1.4:33.3:
It is because they are not strong that when access has arisen, the mind now makes the sign its object and now re-enters
the life-continuum, just as when a young child is lifted up and stood on its feet, it repeatedly falls down on the ground.
vsm1.4:33.4: But the factors are strong in absorption.
vsm1.4:33.5:
It is because they are strong that when absorption concentration has arisen, the mind, having once interrupted
the flow of the life-continuum, carries on with a stream of profitable impulsion for a whole night and for a whole day,
just as a healthy man, after rising from his seat, could stand for a whole day.
vsm1.4:34.1: The arousing of the counterpart sign, which arises together with access concentration, is very difficult.
vsm1.4:34.2: Therefore if he is able to arrive at absorption in that same session by extending the sign, it is good.
vsm1.4:34.3: If not, then he must guard the sign diligently as if it were the foetus of a Wheel-turning Monarch (World-ruler).
vsm1.4:34.4:
So guard the sign, nor count the cost,
And what is gained will not be lost;
vsm1.4:34.5:
Who fails to have this guard maintained
Will lose each time what he has gained.
vsm1.4:35.1: Herein, the way of guarding it is this:
vsm1.4:35.2:
(1) Abode, (2) resort, (3) and speech, (4) and person,
(5) The food, (6) the climate, (7) and the posture—
vsm1.4:35.3:
Eschew these seven different kinds
Whenever found unsuitable.
vsm1.4:35.4:
But cultivate the suitable;
For one perchance so doing finds
He need not wait too long until
Absorption shall his wish fulfil.
vsm1.4:36.1: Herein, an abode is unsuitable if, while he lives in it,
vsm1.4:36.2: the unarisen sign does not arise in him
vsm1.4:36.3: or is lost when it arises,
vsm1.4:36.4: and where unestablished mindfulness fails to become established
vsm1.4:36.5: and the unconcentrated mind fails to become concentrated.
vsm1.4:36.6: That is suitable in which the sign arises and becomes confirmed,
vsm1.4:36.9: as in the Elder Padhāniya-Tissa, resident at Nāgapabbata.
vsm1.4:36.10: So if a monastery has many abodes he can try them one by one,
vsm1.4:36.11: living in each for three days,
vsm1.4:36.12: and stay on where his mind becomes unified.
vsm1.4:36.13: For it was due to suitability of abode that
vsm1.4:36.14:
five hundred bhikkhus reached Arahantship while still dwelling in the Lesser Nāga Cave
(Cūḷa-nāga-leṇa) in Tambapaṇṇi Island (Sri Lanka) after apprehending their meditation subject there.
vsm1.4:36.15: There is no counting the stream-enterers who have reached Arahantship there after reaching the noble plane elsewhere;
vsm1.4:36.16: so too in the monastery of Cittalapabbata, and others.
vsm1.4:37.1: An alms-resort village lying to the north or south of the lodging,
vsm1.4:37.2: not too far, within one kosa and a half,
vsm1.4:37.3: and where alms food is easily obtained, is suitable.
vsm1.4:38.1: Speech: that included in the thirty-two kinds of aimless talk is unsuitable; for it leads to the disappearance of the sign.
vsm1.4:38.2: But talk based on the ten examples of talk is suitable, though even that should be discussed with moderation.
vsm1.4:39.1: Person: one not given to aimless talk, who has the special qualities of virtue, etc.,
vsm1.4:39.2: by acquaintanceship with whom the unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated,
vsm1.4:39.3: or the concentrated mind becomes more so,
vsm1.4:39.5: One who is much concerned with his body, who is addicted to aimless talk, is unsuitable;
vsm1.4:39.6: for he only creates disturbances, like muddy water added to clear water.
vsm1.4:39.7: And it was owing to one such as this that
vsm1.4:39.8: the attainments of the young bhikkhu who lived at Koṭapabbata vanished,
vsm1.4:40.1: Food: Sweet food suits one, sour food another.
vsm1.4:40.2: Climate: a cool climate suits one, a warm one another.
vsm1.4:40.3: So when he finds that by using certain food or by living in a certain climate he is comfortable,
vsm1.4:40.4: or his unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated,
vsm1.4:40.5: or his concentrated mind becomes more so,
vsm1.4:40.6: then that food or that climate is suitable.
vsm1.4:40.7: Any other food or climate is unsuitable.
vsm1.4:41.1: Postures: walking suits one; standing or sitting or lying down suits another.
vsm1.4:41.2: So he should try them, like the abode, for three days each,
vsm1.4:41.3: and that posture is suitable in which his unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated
vsm1.4:41.4: or his concentrated mind becomes more so.
vsm1.4:41.5: Any other should be understood as unsuitable.
vsm1.4:41.6: So he should avoid the seven unsuitable kinds and cultivate the suitable.
vsm1.4:41.7: For when he practices in this way,
vsm1.4:41.9: then, “he need not wait too long until absorption shall his wish fulfil.”
